name: Spire Don't Grieve (For What It Never Owned)
description:
Released in 2196 by the artist known only as Thresh — later identified as Yusuf Abara-Kowalczyk, a former Vantablack Media session musician who had moved to the Shelf after a contract dispute — 'Spire Don't Grieve' was recorded in a single session in a Shelf District 7 dive bar using a handheld recorder and pressed onto forty ceramic data chips that Thresh distributed personally at three funerals in the same week. The song is built on a slow, processional groove derived from New Orleans second-line rhythms filtered through Malian ngoni drone and Norwegian hardanger fiddle harmonics, performed here on a heavily modified steel guitar strung with industrial cable.

The title is addressed to the Spire — the ultra-elite tier of GLMZ — but the song is not angry. It is something harder to categorize: a formal statement of separation, almost ceremonial in its calm. 'We bury our own / in the cold of the Shelf / no flowers from you / no words for ourselves / Spire don't grieve / for what it never owned.' It became the standard closing song at Shelf funerals within two years of its release, spreading entirely through community transmission. It is also, notably, played at Circuit funerals for workers who died in corporate accidents — a slightly different tradition, in which the song is understood as an accusation rather than a declaration of autonomy.
creator: Thresh
genre: Shelf funeral standard, processional, industrial folk blues
audience: Shelf communities, Circuit workers, labor communities, anyone burying someone the city doesn't think matters
cultural_impact: The song's gray-market status — it was never formally banned, but Thresh's identification as a former Vantablack session musician led to quiet industry pressure that kept it off licensed feeds — became itself part of its meaning. To play it at a funeral is to acknowledge that the deceased lived outside the systems that would have granted them visibility. Grief researchers studying GLMZ cite the song as evidence that Shelf communities have developed robust, self-sufficient mourning cultures that explicitly exclude corporate or Spire-tier participation. A bootleg live recording of Thresh performing it at a mass funeral after the Shelf District 4 structural collapse of 2201 is considered one of the most significant documents of early 23rd century GLMZ social history.
known_fans: anyone who has buried someone in the lower tiers
story_hooks: Thresh — Yusuf Abara-Kowalczyk — has agreed to perform 'Spire Don't Grieve' live for the first time in fifteen years at a mass memorial for victims of a recent corporate disaster, but Vantablack Media is applying pressure to prevent the performance, and someone needs to make sure it happens.

A Tier 5 executive's child, estranged from their family and living in Shelf District 3 under a false name, has died — and the community wants to honor them with the song. The executive has learned of this and is sending people to stop it, unable to bear the implication.

The original forty ceramic data chips Thresh pressed in 2196 are considered sacred objects in several Shelf District 7 families. Someone has begun collecting them — buying, stealing, or coercing — and no one yet knows why, but thirty-seven of the forty have already changed hands.
